title: What It Feels Like to Study Abroad: Real Stories
summary: Curious about what it feels like to study abroad? From culture shock to lifelong friendships, here are real experiences every student should know before going.
body_markdown:
[Living Abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/living-abroad/)


You’ve probably daydreamed about it, maybe even Googled it at 2 a.m. while staring at your ceiling. Packing your bags, boarding a plane, and starting a whole new chapter in a foreign country, it sounds equal parts thrilling and terrifying. And honestly? It is both. If you’re wondering **what it feels like to study abroad** , the honest answer is that it’s nothing like what the brochures show, and it’s so much better (and harder) than you expect. If you’re still in the planning stage, check out[How to Study Abroad from Indonesia: A Complete Guide](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-study-abroad-from-indonesia/) to get your foundations right.


This article is for anyone who’s curious, nervous, or on the fence. We’re pulling back the curtain with real talk, real feelings, and real experiences from students who’ve actually done it.

##


**The First Few Weeks: Exciting and Overwhelming at the Same Time**


Most students describe the first month abroad as a complete emotional rollercoaster. One day you’re buzzing with excitement, exploring a new city and meeting people from all over the world. The next day you’re sitting alone in your dorm room wondering why you thought this was a good idea.


###


**1. The Honeymoon Phase Is Real**


The first week or two feels almost magical. Everything is new, everything is interesting, and you’re running on pure adrenaline. You’re taking photos of street signs, trying weird snacks, and saying yes to every social invitation because you don’t want to miss a thing.


This phase is beautiful. Soak it in while it lasts.


###


**2. Then Culture Shock Hits**


Culture shock doesn’t always look like what you imagine. It’s not just struggling with a new language or eating unfamiliar food. Sometimes it’s the tiny things, like not knowing the unwritten rules of the classroom, feeling awkward in social situations, or missing the way your mom cooks rice.


*Culture shock* can feel like a low-grade exhaustion that’s hard to explain. You’re not sick, you’re not sad exactly, but something just feels off. This is completely normal, and nearly every international student goes through it.


###


**3. Loneliness Is Part of the Journey**


No one talks about this enough. Even the most outgoing people feel lonely when they first move abroad. Building real friendships takes time, and in the beginning, you might feel like everyone else has already found their people except you. Hang in there. It changes.


##


**What the Academic Experience Actually Feels Like**


Studying abroad isn’t just about travel and Instagram moments. There’s real academic pressure, and the learning style abroad can be very different from what you’re used to back home.


###


**1. Classes Are Often More Interactive**


In many Western and Asian universities, professors expect students to speak up, ask questions, and challenge ideas out loud. If you’re used to a more passive learning style, this can feel uncomfortable at first. But it’s one of the most valuable things you’ll adapt to, because it pushes you to think critically and communicate with confidence.


###


**2. The Workload Can Catch You Off Guard**


Group projects, research papers, presentations, and tight deadlines, all in a language that might not be your first. It’s a lot. Time management becomes your best friend. Students who struggle most are often those who underestimate the academic side of studying abroad and over-prioritize the travel side.


###


**3. You Discover How You Actually Learn**


Being away from home strips away all your familiar comfort zones, including your academic ones. You figure out how you study best, what motivates you, and what your actual intellectual interests are. Many students say they became genuinely passionate about their field while studying abroad, often because the environment pushed them to engage more deeply.


##


**The Personal Growth Nobody Warned You About**


Here’s the part that’s hard to describe until you live it. Studying abroad changes you as a person, quietly and profoundly. It’s not dramatic. It’s more like you come back and realize you see the world differently.


###


**1. Your Independence Skyrockets**


You learn to[navigate life abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/living-abroad-tips/) on your own: cooking, budgeting, handling bureaucracy in a foreign language, and making decisions without your parents a phone call away. It’s scary at first, but incredibly empowering. Most students say this is the biggest personal shift they experience.


###


**2. Your Perspective on Your Home Country Changes**


Distance gives you clarity. You start to see your home culture from the outside, appreciating things you took for granted and questioning things you once accepted without thinking. Many Indonesian students studying abroad develop a much deeper love for their roots alongside a broader global worldview.


###


**3. You Build Friendships That Last Decades**


The friends you make while studying abroad are a special kind. You’re all going through something intense and new together, which creates a bond that’s hard to replicate elsewhere. These connections often span continents and last a lifetime.


###


**4. You Learn to Handle Money Differently**


Living abroad on a student budget is a crash course in[financial literacy](https://blog.transfez.com/en/why-financial-literacy-is-important/) . You track spending, learn to prioritize, and figure out how to manage international transfers when you need support from home. Apps like Transfez can make sending and receiving money across borders simpler, so you can focus on your studies instead of stressing about logistics.


##


**What Students Wish They Had Known Before Going**


We asked around, and these are the real things students wish someone had told them before they boarded that flight.


- **Your comfort zone will be shattered.** That’s the whole point. Embrace it instead of fighting it.
- **Call home, but not too much.** Staying connected is healthy, but over-relying on home can slow your adjustment.
- **Learn a few phrases in the local language.** Even a basic effort goes a long way in earning respect and making friends.
- **Don’t compare your experience to others’ highlight reels.** Social media shows the best moments. Everyone has hard days.
- **Get your visa and paperwork sorted early.** Bureaucracy is the least fun part of studying abroad, but ignoring it can derail everything. Read up on[how to get a visa](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-get-a-visa/) well in advance.
- **Open a local bank account as soon as possible.** It makes daily life so much easier. Here’s a guide on[how to open a bank account abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-open-a-bank-account-abroad/) .

Studying abroad is one of those experiences that’s genuinely hard to put into words until you’re living it. It stretches you, humbles you, and ultimately shapes you into a version of yourself you didn’t know was possible. The homesickness is real, the growth is real, and the memories are the kind you’ll be telling stories about for the rest of your life. If you’re on the edge of the decision, consider this your gentle nudge: go. You’ll figure it out as you go, and you’ll be better for it.
